claim: Telomerase RNA (TR) provides the template for DNA repeat synthesis at telomeres.
source: Telomerase RNA (TR) provides the template for DNA repeat synthesis at telomeres and is essential for genome stability in continuously dividing cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of telomere biology, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Telomerase RNA is essential for genome stability in continuously dividing cells.
source: Telomerase RNA (TR) provides the template for DNA repeat synthesis at telomeres and is essential for genome stability in continuously dividing cells.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific consensus in telomere biology.

claim: The study mapped the RNA interactome of human TR (hTR).
source: We mapped the RNA interactome of human TR (hTR) and identified a set of non-coding and coding hTR-interacting RNAs, including the histone 1C mRNA (HIST1H1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study identified a set of non-coding and coding hTR-interacting RNAs, including the histone 1C mRNA (HIST1H1C).
source: We mapped the RNA interactome of human TR (hTR) and identified a set of non-coding and coding hTR-interacting RNAs, including the histone 1C mRNA (HIST1H1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the RAP-RNA[FA] RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disruption of the hTR-HIST1H1C RNA association resulted in markedly increased telomere elongation without affecting telomerase enzymatic activity.
source: Disruption of the hTR-HIST1H1C RNA association resulted in markedly increased telomere elongation without affecting telomerase enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the telomere length analysis and telomerase activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Over-expression of HIST1H1C led to telomere attrition.
source: Conversely, over-expression of HIST1H1C led to telomere attrition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the telomere length analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HIST1H1C RNA negatively regulates telomere length independently of its protein coding potential.
source: By using a combination of mutations to disentangle the effects of histone 1 RNA synthesis, protein expression, and hTR interaction, we show that HIST1H1C RNA negatively regulates telomere length independently of its protein coding potential.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments using silent mutations and frameshift constructs presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most human cells display progressive telomere shortening during cell divisions.
source: Most human cells display progressive telomere shortening during cell divisions, ultimately resulting in replicative senescence or apoptosis (Harley et al., 1990; Maciejowski and de Lange, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Progressive telomere shortening ultimately results in replicative senescence or apoptosis.
source: Most human cells display progressive telomere shortening during cell divisions, ultimately resulting in replicative senescence or apoptosis (Harley et al., 1990; Maciejowski and de Lange, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the majority of cancer cells and in continuously dividing germ line cells, telomere erosion is mitigated by the action of telomerase.
source: In the majority of cancer cells and in continuously dividing germ line cells, however, telomere erosion is mitigated by the action of telomerase – a specialized ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex minimally composed of telomerase RNA (TR) and the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) enzyme.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field of telomere biology.

claim: Telomerase is a specialized ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex minimally composed of telomerase RNA (TR) and the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) enzyme.
source: In the majority of cancer cells and in continuously dividing germ line cells, however, telomere erosion is mitigated by the action of telomerase – a specialized ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex minimally composed of telomerase RNA (TR) and the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) enzyme.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field of telomere biology.

claim: Telomere homeostasis depends on the highly regulated co-ordination of telomerase RNP assembly, trafficking, and recruitment to telomeres during the S phase of the cell cycle.
source: Telomere homeostasis depends on the highly regulated co-ordination of telomerase RNP assembly, trafficking, and recruitment to telomeres during the S phase of the cell cycle (Schmidt and Cech, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All TRs contain a short internal template for telomeric DNA repeat synthesis.
source: While all TRs contain a short internal template for telomeric DNA repeat synthesis (Greider and Blackburn, 1989), vertebrate TRs also possess an H/ACA box small Cajal body (CB)-specific RNA (scaRNA) domain (Jády et al., 2004; Mitchell et al., 1999a) (Figure 1A) that associates with the canonical H/ACA scaRNA-binding proteins (Nguyen et al., 2018), including the pseudouridine synthase dyskerin (Mitchell et al., 1999b) and the CB chaperone WDR79/TCAB1 (Tycowski et al., 2009; Venteicher et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Vertebrate TRs possess an H/ACA box small Cajal body (CB)-specific RNA (scaRNA) domain.
source: While all TRs contain a short internal template for telomeric DNA repeat synthesis (Greider and Blackburn, 1989), vertebrate TRs also possess an H/ACA box small Cajal body (CB)-specific RNA (scaRNA) domain (Jády et al., 2004; Mitchell et al., 1999a) (Figure 1A) that associates with the canonical H/ACA scaRNA-binding proteins (Nguyen et al., 2018), including the pseudouridine synthase dyskerin (Mitchell et al., 1999b) and the CB chaperone WDR79/TCAB1 (Tycowski et al., 2009; Venteicher et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The H/ACA scaRNA domain associates with the canonical H/ACA scaRNA-binding proteins, including the pseudouridine synthase dyskerin and the CB chaperone WDR79/TCAB1.
source: While all TRs contain a short internal template for telomeric DNA repeat synthesis (Greider and Blackburn, 1989), vertebrate TRs also possess an H/ACA box small Cajal body (CB)-specific RNA (scaRNA) domain (Jády et al., 2004; Mitchell et al., 1999a) (Figure 1A) that associates with the canonical H/ACA scaRNA-binding proteins (Nguyen et al., 2018), including the pseudouridine synthase dyskerin (Mitchell et al., 1999b) and the CB chaperone WDR79/TCAB1 (Tycowski et al., 2009; Venteicher et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The H/ACA region is required for the correct trafficking, stability, and catalytically active conformation of hTR.
source: The H/ACA region is required for the correct trafficking, stability, and catalytically active conformation of hTR (Chen et al., 2018; Jády et al., 2004; Mitchell et al., 1999a; Zhu et al., 2004) but is considered non-functional as a pseudouridylation guide RNA (Meier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The H/ACA region is considered non-functional as a pseudouridylation guide RNA.
source: The H/ACA region is required for the correct trafficking, stability, and catalytically active conformation of hTR (Chen et al., 2018; Jády et al., 2004; Mitchell et al., 1999a; Zhu et al., 2004) but is considered non-functional as a pseudouridylation guide RNA (Meier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: hTERT expression is silenced in most human somatic cells.
source: Interestingly, while hTERT expression is silenced in most human somatic cells, hTR is broadly expressed in normal tissues (Feng et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: hTR is broadly expressed in normal tissues.
source: Interestingly, while hTERT expression is silenced in most human somatic cells, hTR is broadly expressed in normal tissues (Feng et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: hTR levels are in excess over telomerase RNP complexes in cancer cells.
source: In addition, hTR levels are in excess over telomerase RNP complexes in cancer cells (Xi and Cech, 2014), indicating that a pool of TERT-free hTR might assemble into alternate RNP complexes both in normal and transformed cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A pool of TERT-free hTR might assemble into alternate RNP complexes both in normal and transformed cells.
source: In addition, hTR levels are in excess over telomerase RNP complexes in cancer cells (Xi and Cech, 2014), indicating that a pool of TERT-free hTR might assemble into alternate RNP complexes both in normal and transformed cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that hTR levels exceed telomerase RNP complexes.

claim: Role(s) independent of telomerase activity have been demonstrated for hTR in cell survival and in the regulation of apoptosis.
source: Indeed, role(s) independent of telomerase activity – with as yet poorly defined mechanism(s) – have been demonstrated for hTR in cell survival and in the regulation of apoptosis (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014; Kedde et al., 2006; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cell protective function of hTR was mapped to the 3' H/ACA domain.
source: The cell protective function of hTR was mapped to the 3' H/ACA domain and was shown to be negatively regulated by the formation of catalytically active telomerase RNP complexes (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The cell protective function of hTR is negatively regulated by the formation of catalytically active telomerase RNP complexes.
source: The cell protective function of hTR was mapped to the 3' H/ACA domain and was shown to be negatively regulated by the formation of catalytically active telomerase RNP complexes (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most non-coding RNA classes engage in complementarity-driven base-pairing with other RNAs or DNA.
source: Besides serving as flexible scaffolds for protein binding and RNP assembly, most non-coding RNA classes engage in complementarity-driven base-pairing with other RNAs or DNA (Falaleeva and Stamm, 2013; Tay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: RNA duplex formation has been suggested to regulate messenger RNA localization/compartmentalization.
source: In addition, RNA duplex formation has also been suggested to regulate messenger RNA localization/compartmentalization (Langdon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Several methods for either targeted or transcriptome-wide mapping of RNA-RNA interactions have been reported in recent years.
source: In recent years, several methods for either targeted (Engreitz et al., 2014; Kretz et al., 2013) or transcriptome-wide (Aw et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016) mapping of RNA-RNA interactions have been reported, providing the first glimpses into the intricate RNA interaction network in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The overlap in the identified interactions using different transcriptome-wide methods is rather limited.
source: Although transcriptome-wide methods, relying on psoralen photo-crosslinking and proximity ligation (Aw et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016) have provided important insights into the overall network topology of the RNA interactome, the overlap in the identified interactions using the different methods is rather limited (Gong et al., 2018), suggesting that the current approaches might cover only a fraction of the complex cellular RNA interaction network.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Current approaches might cover only a fraction of the complex cellular RNA interaction network.
source: Although transcriptome-wide methods, relying on psoralen photo-crosslinking and proximity ligation (Aw et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016) have provided important insights into the overall network topology of the RNA interactome, the overlap in the identified interactions using the different methods is rather limited (Gong et al., 2018), suggesting that the current approaches might cover only a fraction of the complex cellular RNA interaction network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited overlap between different methods.

claim: Psoralen-based methods are biased by the sequence- and structural features of RNA duplexes.
source: In addition, psoralen-based methods are also biased by the sequence- and structural features of RNA duplexes, as they preferentially detect interacting regions with staggered uridine bases on opposing strands (Cimino et al., 1985; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Psoralen-based methods preferentially detect interacting regions with staggered uridine bases on opposing strands.
source: In addition, psoralen-based methods are also biased by the sequence- and structural features of RNA duplexes, as they preferentially detect interacting regions with staggered uridine bases on opposing strands (Cimino et al., 1985; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The protein composition of the telomerase RNP has been characterized in detail.
source: While the protein composition (Nguyen et al., 2018) and chromatin-binding sites (Chu et al., 2011) of the telomerase RNP have been characterized in detail, virtually nothing is currently known about RNAs potentially interacting with hTR.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The chromatin-binding sites of the telomerase RNP have been characterized in detail.
source: While the protein composition (Nguyen et al., 2018) and chromatin-binding sites (Chu et al., 2011) of the telomerase RNP have been characterized in detail, virtually nothing is currently known about RNAs potentially interacting with hTR.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Virtually nothing is currently known about RNAs potentially interacting with hTR.
source: While the protein composition (Nguyen et al., 2018) and chromatin-binding sites (Chu et al., 2011) of the telomerase RNP have been characterized in detail, virtually nothing is currently known about RNAs potentially interacting with hTR.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The study mapped the hTR-RNA interaction network by formaldehyde cross-linking followed by RNA antisense purification and RNA sequencing (RAP-RNA[FA] RNA-seq).
source: We mapped the hTR-RNA interaction network by formaldehyde cross-linking followed by RNA antisense purification and RNA sequencing (RAP-RNA[FA] RNA-seq) (Engreitz et al., 2014; the experimental pipeline is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Telomerase RNP formation is expected to compete with some of the alternative functions of hTR.
source: Since telomerase RNP formation is expected to compete with (some of) the alternative functions of hTR (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014; Xi and Cech, 2014) and can also influence hTR trafficking (Tomlinson et al., 2008), we used both hTR-/hTERT- VA13 cells transiently transfected by hTR (VA13-hTR) and hTR+/hTERT+ HeLa cells for hTR antisense purification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Telomerase RNP formation can influence hTR trafficking.
source: Since telomerase RNP formation is expected to compete with (some of) the alternative functions of hTR (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014; Xi and Cech, 2014) and can also influence hTR trafficking (Tomlinson et al., 2008), we used both hTR-/hTERT- VA13 cells transiently transfected by hTR (VA13-hTR) and hTR+/hTERT+ HeLa cells for hTR antisense purification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The study identified 80 RNA species interacting with hTR in VA13-hTR cells.
source: To build a high-confidence set of hTR interacting RNA molecules, only highly (>4 fold) enriched, reproducibly identified peaks were considered further, resulting in 80 RNA species in VA13-hTR cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the RAP-RNA[FA] RNA-seq data.

claim: The stringent filtering criteria resulted in fewer hTR-interacting RNAs in the TERT+ HeLa cells (16 RNA species).
source: As expected, the stringent filtering criteria resulted in fewer hTR-interacting RNAs in the TERT+ HeLa cells (16 RNA species (Figure 1—source data 1), out of which 11 were also enriched in pull-downs from VA13-hTR cells; Figure 1C), in agreement with a possible competition between active telomerase RNP formation and non-canonical interactions (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the experimental data and consistent with previous research.

claim: 11 out of 16 hTR-interacting RNAs identified in HeLa cells were also enriched in pull-downs from VA13-hTR cells.
source: As expected, the stringent filtering criteria resulted in fewer hTR-interacting RNAs in the TERT+ HeLa cells (16 RNA species (Figure 1—source data 1), out of which 11 were also enriched in pull-downs from VA13-hTR cells; Figure 1C), in agreement with a possible competition between active telomerase RNP formation and non-canonical interactions (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the experimental data.

claim: RAP-RNA[FA] can detect both indirect interactions and direct RNA-RNA interactions caged or flanked by proteins.
source: Although RAP-RNA[FA] can detect both indirect interactions and direct RNA-RNA interactions caged or flanked by proteins (Engreitz et al., 2014), prediction of potential duplex formation between hTR and the enriched RNA regions – compared to either the corresponding antisense or shuffled RNA sequences – suggested that the majority of the interactions are mediated by direct RNA-RNA base pairing (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research describing the method.

claim: The majority of the interactions between hTR and enriched RNA regions are mediated by direct RNA-RNA base pairing.
source: Although RAP-RNA[FA] can detect both indirect interactions and direct RNA-RNA interactions caged or flanked by proteins (Engreitz et al., 2014), prediction of potential duplex formation between hTR and the enriched RNA regions – compared to either the corresponding antisense or shuffled RNA sequences – suggested that the majority of the interactions are mediated by direct RNA-RNA base pairing (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions of RNA duplex formation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The predicted interaction sites fall mostly within regions of hTR that are not thought to be involved in the regulation of telomerase activity or trafficking.
source: Interestingly, the predicted interaction sites fall mostly within regions of hTR that are not thought to be involved in the regulation of telomerase activity or trafficking (Figure 2B; indicated in grey in Figure 1A), suggesting that these sequences might function as 'hubs' for RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1A.

claim: The predicted interaction sites in hTR might function as 'hubs' for RNA-RNA interactions.
source: Interestingly, the predicted interaction sites fall mostly within regions of hTR that are not thought to be involved in the regulation of telomerase activity or trafficking (Figure 2B; indicated in grey in Figure 1A), suggesting that these sequences might function as 'hubs' for RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The stringently filtered dataset included HSP90AB1, the only hTR-interacting mRNA identified by the transcriptome-wide LIGR-seq method.
source: Confirming the validity of our approach, the stringently filtered dataset included HSP90AB1, the only hTR-interacting mRNA identified by the transcriptome-wide LIGR-seq method (Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding that validates the approach by comparison with previous research.

claim: Enrichment of selected candidates (TPT1, FLNA, and IFITM3) was successfully verified by qRT-PCR on RAP samples.
source: Furthermore, enrichment of selected candidates, such as TPT1, FLNA, and IFITM3 was successfully verified by qRT-PCR on RAP samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The HIST1H1C transcript, coding for the H1.2 linker histone subtype, was identified as one of the most highly enriched RNAs upon hTR pull-down both in VA13-hTR and HeLa cells.
source: We identified the HIST1H1C transcript, coding for the H1.2 linker histone subtype, as one of the most highly enriched RNAs upon hTR pull-down both in VA13-hTR and HeLa cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the RAP-RNA[FA] RNA-seq data.

claim: Cell-cycle-regulated histone transcripts are processed in histone locus bodies (HLBs).
source: Cell-cycle-regulated histone transcripts are processed in histone locus bodies (HLBs), nuclear structures formed at the sites of histone gene transcription and concentrating factors involved in histone pre-mRNA recognition and maturation (Nizami et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HLBs are nuclear structures formed at the sites of histone gene transcription and concentrating factors involved in histone pre-mRNA recognition and maturation.
source: Cell-cycle-regulated histone transcripts are processed in histone locus bodies (HLBs), nuclear structures formed at the sites of histone gene transcription and concentrating factors involved in histone pre-mRNA recognition and maturation (Nizami et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HLBs generally co-localize with CBs.
source: Although HLBs are highly dynamic in space and time, they generally co-localize with CBs, operationally defined as coilin-positive nuclear foci (Bongiorno-Borbone et al., 2008; Machyna et al., 2014; Nizami et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: hTR has been shown to accumulate in CBs throughout the cell cycle.
source: Interestingly, hTR has also been shown to accumulate in CBs throughout the cell cycle (Jády et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2004), and to be recruited to telomeres specifically in S phase (Jády et al., 2006; Tomlinson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: hTR is recruited to telomeres specifically in S phase.
source: Interestingly, hTR has also been shown to accumulate in CBs throughout the cell cycle (Jády et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2004), and to be recruited to telomeres specifically in S phase (Jády et al., 2006; Tomlinson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prediction of potential base-pairing between HIST1H1C and hTR identified a 15-nt long region in the open reading frame (ORF) of HIST1H1C (nts 334–348) complementary to the terminal stem-loop sequence of the P6b region of hTR.
source: Prediction of potential base-pairing between HIST1H1C and hTR identified a 15-nt long region in the open reading frame (ORF) of HIST1H1C (nts 334–348) complementary to the terminal stem-loop sequence of the P6b region of hTR (Figure 3C), suggesting a direct RNA-RNA interaction between the two RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 15-nt long region in HIST1H1C complementary to hTR was named TRIAGE, for telomerase RNA interacting genetic element.
source: We named this 15-nt long region TRIAGE, for telomerase RNA interacting genetic element.
evidence: This is a definition introduced by the authors.

claim: The recently published cryo-EM structure of human telomerase RNP indicated that the P6b region is exposed and accessible in the holoenzyme.
source: The recently published cryo-EM structure of human telomerase RNP (Nguyen et al., 2018) indicated that the P6b region is exposed and accessible in the holoenzyme.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Enrichment of HIST1H1C upon hTR pull-down was abrogated in all P6b mutants.
source: Importantly, enrichment of HIST1H1C upon hTR pull-down was abrogated in all P6b mutants (Figure 3D), including hTR-RS, indicating that sequence complementarity is necessary but not sufficient for the specific RNA-RNA interaction between the P6b stem-loop and the HIST1H1C transcript.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Sequence complementarity is necessary but not sufficient for the specific RNA-RNA interaction between the P6b stem-loop and the HIST1H1C transcript.
source: Importantly, enrichment of HIST1H1C upon hTR pull-down was abrogated in all P6b mutants (Figure 3D), including hTR-RS, indicating that sequence complementarity is necessary but not sufficient for the specific RNA-RNA interaction between the P6b stem-loop and the HIST1H1C transcript.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that the RS mutant did not restore the interaction.

claim: HIST1H1B mRNA contains the exact TRIAGE sequence but was enriched upon hTR pull-down to a much lesser extent than its HIST1H1C paralog.
source: In agreement with this, HIST1H1B mRNA contains the exact TRIAGE sequence (Figure 3C) but was enriched upon hTR pull-down to a much lesser extent than its HIST1H1C paralog (Figure 3A), suggesting that features besides base complementarity (e.g. secondary structure of the mRNA, specific protein binding etc.) determine the interaction.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3C.

claim: Features besides base complementarity (e.g. secondary structure of the mRNA, specific protein binding etc.) determine the hTR-HIST1H1C interaction.
source: In agreement with this, HIST1H1B mRNA contains the exact TRIAGE sequence (Figure 3C) but was enriched upon hTR pull-down to a much lesser extent than its HIST1H1C paralog (Figure 3A), suggesting that features besides base complementarity (e.g. secondary structure of the mRNA, specific protein binding etc.) determine the interaction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: H1.2 protein levels were not significantly affected by hTR or variant hTR expression.
source: As H1.2 protein levels were not significantly affected by hTR or variant hTR expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we determined whether the HIST1H1C-hTR interaction might play a role in the regulation of telomere homeostasis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous hTR levels in HT1080 cells are more limiting in telomere elongation compared to other widely used cancer cell lines.
source: Endogenous hTR levels in HT1080 cells are more limiting in telomere elongation compared to other widely used cancer cell lines, enabling the characterization of mutant hTRs (Cristofari and Lingner, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The m1 hTR mutant (containing the G414C mutation) fails to accumulate in CBs and causes reduced telomere lengthening in HT1080 cells.
source: We also included the well-characterized m1 hTR mutant (containing the G414C mutation), which fails to accumulate in CBs and causes reduced telomere lengthening in HT1080 cells (Cristofari et al., 2007; Jády et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: All hTR variants could be stably over-expressed, resulting in ~3–4 fold hTR expression over endogenous levels.
source: All hTR variants could be stably over-expressed, resulting in ~3–4 fold hTR expression over endogenous levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of the terminal stem-loop of the P6b region strongly reduced telomerase activity.
source: While deletion of the terminal stem-loop of the P6b region strongly reduced telomerase activity, hTR variants that conserved the overall RNA secondary structure (SW and RS) showed telomerase activities comparable to wild-type hTR, indicating that neither the sequence of the P6b stem-loop nor its interaction with HIST1H1C RNA are required for catalytically active telomerase RNP assembly (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the qTRAP assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: hTR variants that conserved the overall RNA secondary structure (SW and RS) showed telomerase activities comparable to wild-type hTR.
source: While deletion of the terminal stem-loop of the P6b region strongly reduced telomerase activity, hTR variants that conserved the overall RNA secondary structure (SW and RS) showed telomerase activities comparable to wild-type hTR, indicating that neither the sequence of the P6b stem-loop nor its interaction with HIST1H1C RNA are required for catalytically active telomerase RNP assembly (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the qTRAP assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neither the sequence of the P6b stem-loop nor its interaction with HIST1H1C RNA are required for catalytically active telomerase RNP assembly.
source: While deletion of the terminal stem-loop of the P6b region strongly reduced telomerase activity, hTR variants that conserved the overall RNA secondary structure (SW and RS) showed telomerase activities comparable to wild-type hTR, indicating that neither the sequence of the P6b stem-loop nor its interaction with HIST1H1C RNA are required for catalytically active telomerase RNP assembly (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Substitution of the terminal stem-loop for the GAAA tetraloop sequence showed no influence on telomerase enzymatic activity.
source: This is in agreement with a previous report, where substitution of the terminal stem-loop for the GAAA tetraloop sequence showed no influence on telomerase enzymatic activity (Mitchell and Collins, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The enzymatic activity associated with hTR variants measured in cell lysates does not necessarily correlate with productive telomere elongation.
source: The enzymatic activity associated with hTR variants measured in cell lysates reflects the assembly of telomerase RNPs but – owing to potential trafficking defects – does not necessarily correlate with productive telomere elongation, as previously shown for hTR m1 (Cristofari et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Expression of hTR variants did not change the cell growth characteristics.
source: Expression of hTR variants did not change the cell growth characteristics (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the population doubling data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Wild-type hTR over-expression resulted in a steady increase in MTL (averaging ~82 nt per population doubling).
source: As expected, wild-type hTR over-expression resulted in a steady increase in MTL (averaging ~82 nt per population doubling), while U1 promoter alone, the catalytically compromised ΔP6 hTR variant or m1 hTR expression did not result in significant telomere elongation (Figure 4D and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the TRF analysis data shown in Figure 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: U1 promoter alone, the catalytically compromised ΔP6 hTR variant or m1 hTR expression did not result in significant telomere elongation.
source: As expected, wild-type hTR over-expression resulted in a steady increase in MTL (averaging ~82 nt per population doubling), while U1 promoter alone, the catalytically compromised ΔP6 hTR variant or m1 hTR expression did not result in significant telomere elongation (Figure 4D and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the TRF analysis data shown in Figure 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell lines over-expressing either the SW or RS variant displayed markedly increased telomere lengthening compared to wild-type hTR.
source: Surprisingly, cell lines over-expressing either the SW or RS variant displayed markedly increased telomere lengthening compared to wild-type hTR (Figure 4D and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the identified HIST1H1C-hTR interaction might interfere with the telomeric activity of the telomerase RNP.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the TRF analysis data shown in Figure 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The identified HIST1H1C-hTR interaction might interfere with the telomeric activity of the telomerase RNP.
source: Surprisingly, cell lines over-expressing either the SW or RS variant displayed markedly increased telomere lengthening compared to wild-type hTR (Figure 4D and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the identified HIST1H1C-hTR interaction might interfere with the telomeric activity of the telomerase RNP.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Silent codon changes were introduced in the TRIAGE region, disrupting complementarity to the P6b stem-loop sequence of hTR, but maintaining its coding potential.
source: Several silent codon changes were introduced in the TRIAGE region, disrupting complementarity to the P6b stem-loop sequence of hTR (Figure 5A), but maintaining its coding potential (silentHIST1H1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Moderate over-expression of 3xFLAG-H1.2 was achieved compared to endogenous H1.2 levels, with similar expression levels for 3xFLAG-H1.2 encoded by the wild-type HIST1H1C sequence and the silentHIST1H1C variant.
source: We achieved moderate over-expression of 3xFLAG-H1.2 compared to endogenous H1.2 levels, with similar expression levels for 3xFLAG-H1.2 encoded by the wild-type HIST1H1C sequence and the silentHIST1H1C variant (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cancer cells maintain a remarkable telomere length equilibrium over a long period ex vivo.
source: While cancer cells maintain a remarkable telomere length equilibrium over a long period ex vivo (Figure 4D and E), over-expression of wtHIST1H1C resulted in telomere attrition and accumulation of short telomeres in all three cell lines after 34 population doublings (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Over-expression of wtHIST1H1C resulted in telomere attrition and accumulation of short telomeres in all three cell lines after 34 population doublings.
source: While cancer cells maintain a remarkable telomere length equilibrium over a long period ex vivo (Figure 4D and E), over-expression of wtHIST1H1C resulted in telomere attrition and accumulation of short telomeres in all three cell lines after 34 population doublings (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the TRF analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: silentHIST1H1C expression had no effect on the MTL.
source: Importantly, silentHIST1H1C expression had no effect on the MTL (Figure 5C), demonstrating that the presence of the TRIAGE sequence is responsible for the observed phenotype, possibly regulating telomere length via the HIST1H1C-hTR RNA-RNA interaction, independently of H1.2 protein expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the TRF analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The presence of the TRIAGE sequence is responsible for the observed telomere attrition phenotype.
source: Importantly, silentHIST1H1C expression had no effect on the MTL (Figure 5C), demonstrating that the presence of the TRIAGE sequence is responsible for the observed phenotype, possibly regulating telomere length via the HIST1H1C-hTR RNA-RNA interaction, independently of H1.2 protein expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between wtHIST1H1C and silentHIST1H1C.

claim: HIST1H1C possibly regulates telomere length via the HIST1H1C-hTR RNA-RNA interaction, independently of H1.2 protein expression.
source: Importantly, silentHIST1H1C expression had no effect on the MTL (Figure 5C), demonstrating that the presence of the TRIAGE sequence is responsible for the observed phenotype, possibly regulating telomere length via the HIST1H1C-hTR RNA-RNA interaction, independently of H1.2 protein expression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: HIST1H1C over-expression had no influence on telomerase enzymatic activity measured in cell lysates.
source: HIST1H1C over-expression had no influence on telomerase enzymatic activity measured in cell lysates (Figure 5E), suggesting that the TRIAGE sequence is affecting a step following telomerase RNP assembly.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the qTRAP assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The TRIAGE sequence is affecting a step following telomerase RNP assembly.
source: HIST1H1C over-expression had no influence on telomerase enzymatic activity measured in cell lysates (Figure 5E), suggesting that the TRIAGE sequence is affecting a step following telomerase RNP assembly.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Two of the three polyclonal wtHIST1H1C-expressing cell lines lost transgene expression upon long-term culture (assessed at 120 days post-transfection).
source: Strikingly, two of the three polyclonal wtHIST1H1C-expressing cell lines, but none of the silentHIST1H1C-expressing cell lines, lost transgene expression upon long-term culture (assessed at 120 days post-transfection; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: None of the silentHIST1H1C-expressing cell lines lost transgene expression upon long-term culture.
source: Strikingly, two of the three polyclonal wtHIST1H1C-expressing cell lines, but none of the silentHIST1H1C-expressing cell lines, lost transgene expression upon long-term culture (assessed at 120 days post-transfection; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cells without (or with very low levels of) H1.2 over-expression might possess a substantial survival advantage.
source: This strong selection pressure prevented us from reliably assessing the influence of TRIAGE-mediated telomere shortening on cell physiology in this model system, and suggested that cells without (or with very low levels of) H1.2 over-expression might possess a substantial survival advantage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Cell line 1 maintaining wild-type H1.2 over-expression exhibited increased p53 protein levels, indicative of DNA damage response activation in this cell population.
source: In agreement with this, cell line 1 – maintaining wild-type H1.2 over-expression (Figure 5D, lane 4) – exhibited increased p53 protein levels, indicative of DNA damage response activation in this cell population.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Only 12 out of 24 clones showed >20% upregulation in their HIST1H1C RNA levels relative to the baseline expression measured in mock-transfected cells.
source: Although most clones expressed detectable levels of 3xFLAG-H1.2 protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), only 12 out of 24 clones showed >20% upregulation in their HIST1H1C RNA levels (Figure 6A) relative to the baseline expression measured in mock-transfected cells.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HIST1H1C over-expression in the clonal cell lines was generally associated with shorter MTL and a higher frequency of short telomeres.
source: HIST1H1C over-expression in the clonal cell lines was generally associated with shorter MTL and a higher frequency of short telomeres (Figure 6B and C, red and orange lines and circles and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the TeSLA data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: An increase in cells undergoing cellular senescence was observed in cell lines with HIST1H1C over-expression.
source: In agreement with the accumulation of shorter telomeres, we observed an increase in cells undergoing cellular senescence, as measured by β-galactosidase staining at two time points (8 weeks and 10 weeks post-transfection) (Figure 6D and E, red and orange circles).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: hTR expression did not correlate with cellular senescence.
source: Interestingly, hTR expression did not correlate with cellular senescence (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that clonal variations in hTR levels are not limiting for the maintenance of the shortest telomeres in this setting.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clonal variations in hTR levels are not limiting for the maintenance of the shortest telomeres in this setting.
source: Interestingly, hTR expression did not correlate with cellular senescence (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that clonal variations in hTR levels are not limiting for the maintenance of the shortest telomeres in this setting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between hTR expression and cellular senescence.

claim: All cell lines over-expressing FS_HIST1H1C (with wild-type TRIAGE sequence) had significantly shorter telomeres (on average by ~700 nt) than the FS_silentHIST1H1C-transfected controls by 3 months.
source: Although there was no statistically significant difference in MTL between the FS_HIST1H1C and FS_silentHIST1H1C-transfected cells at 1 month post-transfection (p=0.62), by 3 months, all cell lines over-expressing FS_HIST1H1C (with wild-type TRIAGE sequence) had significantly shorter telomeres (on average by ~700 nt, p=0.011) than the FS_silentHIST1H1C-transfected controls (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the TeSLA data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: HIST1H1C RNA acts at a step downstream of RNP assembly, possibly by sequestering the active telomerase complex and preventing its proper intranuclear targeting or recruitment to telomeres.
source: As neither HIST1H1C over-expression, nor mutations in the P6b stem-loop of hTR disrupting HIST1H1C association had an effect on telomerase enzymatic activity, we propose that HIST1H1C regulates telomere length homeostasis acting at a step downstream of RNP assembly, possibly by sequestering the active telomerase complex and preventing its proper intranuclear targeting or recruitment to telomeres.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The interaction between hTR and HIST1H1C mRNA might possibly take place in Cajal bodies.
source: As both hTR and replication-dependent histone (pre)mRNAs accumulate in Cajal bodies (Bongiorno-Borbone et al., 2008; Machyna et al., 2014; Jády et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2004), the interaction between the two RNAs might possibly take place in these structures.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the known localization of both RNAs.

claim: The human genome encodes 11 histone 1 (H1) subtypes, five of which (HIST1H1A to HIST1H1E) are located in the large HIST1 gene cluster on chromosome 6.
source: The human genome encodes 11 histone 1 (H1) subtypes, five of which (HIST1H1A to HIST1H1E) are located – along with a number of core histone genes – in the large HIST1 gene cluster on chromosome 6, and are expressed in a cell cycle-dependent fashion in somatic cells (Harshman et al., 2013; Hergeth and Schneider, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HIST1H1A to HIST1H1E are expressed in a cell cycle-dependent fashion in somatic cells.
source: The human genome encodes 11 histone 1 (H1) subtypes, five of which (HIST1H1A to HIST1H1E) are located – along with a number of core histone genes – in the large HIST1 gene cluster on chromosome 6, and are expressed in a cell cycle-dependent fashion in somatic cells (Harshman et al., 2013; Hergeth and Schneider, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: H1 subtypes present cell cycle, cell type, and tissue-specific differences in their expression patterns.
source: H1 subtypes present cell cycle, cell type, and tissue-specific differences in their expression patterns, and their relative ratios undergo profound changes during differentiation, malignant transformation, cancer progression, or under distinct physiological conditions (Happel et al., 2009; Hergeth and Schneider, 2015; Izzo et al., 2017; Pan and Fan, 2016; Scaffidi, 2016; Terme et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The TRIAGE sequence is conserved between HIST1H1C and HIST1H1B.
source: Interestingly, the TRIAGE sequence is conserved between HIST1H1C and HIST1H1B, and shows only one nucleotide difference in HIST1H1E, maintaining complementarity to hTR through G-U base pairing (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The TRIAGE sequence shows only one nucleotide difference in HIST1H1E, maintaining complementarity to hTR through G-U base pairing.
source: Interestingly, the TRIAGE sequence is conserved between HIST1H1C and HIST1H1B, and shows only one nucleotide difference in HIST1H1E, maintaining complementarity to hTR through G-U base pairing (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Some enrichment in hTR pull-downs was observed for HIST1H1B and HIST1H1E, but a preferential enrichment of HIST1H1C mRNA over the other variants was consistently detected.
source: Although we observed some enrichment in hTR pull-downs for these two subtypes (and none for HIST1H1D with two nucleotides difference in the TRIAGE sequence), we consistently detected a preferential enrichment of HIST1H1C mRNA over the other variants.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the experimental data.

claim: The specificity for HIST1H1C could potentially be explained by different intramolecular RNA secondary structures involving the TRIAGE sequence in HIST1H1B and HIST1H1E, or by the involvement of an RNA-binding protein preferentially associating with the HIST1H1C mRNA.
source: The reason for this specificity is currently unclear, but could potentially be explained by different intramolecular RNA secondary structures involving the TRIAGE sequence in HIST1H1B and HIST1H1E, or by the involvement of an RNA-binding protein – preferentially associating with the HIST1H1C mRNA – facilitating the TRIAGE-P6b RNA duplex formation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Under different conditions or in different cell/tissue types HIST1H1B and/or HIST1H1E might more efficiently interact with hTR and regulate its function(s).
source: Nevertheless, it remains possible that under different conditions or in different cell/tissue types HIST1H1B and/or HIST1H1E might more efficiently interact with hTR and regulate its function(s).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future findings.

claim: Linker histones have been implicated in a wide variety of cellular processes, including the specific regulation of gene expression, apoptosis and the DNA damage response.
source: Beyond their role in regulating chromosome condensation as structural constituents of chromatin, linker histones have been implicated in a wide variety of cellular processes (reviewed in Hergeth and Schneider, 2015), including the specific regulation of gene expression, apoptosis and the DNA damage response.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: H1.2 has been shown to repress p53-mediated transcriptional activation of target genes through a direct interaction with p53.
source: For example, H1.2 has been shown to repress p53-mediated transcriptional activation of target genes through – in part – a direct interaction with p53 (Kim et al., 2008; Nishiyama et al., 2009), conferring an anti-apoptotic function upon DNA damage (Nishiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: H1.2 confers an anti-apoptotic function upon DNA damage.
source: For example, H1.2 has been shown to repress p53-mediated transcriptional activation of target genes through – in part – a direct interaction with p53 (Kim et al., 2008; Nishiyama et al., 2009), conferring an anti-apoptotic function upon DNA damage (Nishiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The release of H1.2 from chromatin in response to DNA double-strand breaks has been shown to lead to its translocation to the cytoplasm and to result in the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway and increased cell death in a Bak-dependent manner.
source: In contrast, the release of H1.2 from chromatin in response to DNA double-strand breaks has been shown to lead to its translocation to the cytoplasm and to result in the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway and increased cell death in a Bak-dependent manner (Garg et al., 2014; Konishi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Chromatin compaction states, regulated by linker histone abundance, might influence various fundamental cellular processes, including the DNA damage response and transcription from heterochromatic repeat regions.
source: Chromatin compaction states, regulated by linker histone abundance, might also influence various fundamental cellular processes, including the DNA damage response (Murga et al., 2007; Sulli et al., 2012) and transcription from heterochromatic repeat regions (Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017), potentially modulating telomere length homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Two lines of triple knockout mouse embryonic stem cells lacking H1.2, H1.3 and H1.4 expression showed increased telomere length compared to lines expressing wild-type levels of linker histones.
source: Murga and co-workers reported two lines of triple knockout mouse embryonic stem cells [TKO mES cells, lacking H1.2, H1.3 and H1.4 expression (Fan et al., 2003)] that showed increased telomere length compared to lines expressing wild-type levels of linker histones (Murga et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The increased telomere length in TKO mES cells might be attributed to an ALT-like phenotype due to increased homologous recombination occurring in the relaxed chromatin environment caused by the drastic reduction in H1 histone expression levels.
source: These differences might be attributed to an ALT (alternative lengthening of telomeres)-like phenotype due to increased homologous recombination occurring in the relaxed chromatin environment caused by the drastic reduction in H1 histone expression levels (Murga et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The sequence of the P6b stem-loop is highly conserved in most placental mammals.
source: Interestingly, although the sequence of the P6b stem-loop (as well as that of the TRIAGE sequence) is highly conserved in most placental mammals, mouse and rat P6b is highly divergent, suggesting that the P6b-TRIAGE interaction would not occur in these species.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence analysis.

claim: Mouse and rat P6b is highly divergent, suggesting that the P6b-TRIAGE interaction would not occur in these species.
source: Interestingly, although the sequence of the P6b stem-loop (as well as that of the TRIAGE sequence) is highly conserved in most placental mammals, mouse and rat P6b is highly divergent, suggesting that the P6b-TRIAGE interaction would not occur in these species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on sequence divergence.

claim: The potential lack of the P6b-TRIAGE interaction in mice and rats might reflect divergent evolutionary strategies employed by these short-lived, small species with excessively long telomeres and somatic telomerase activity.
source: Alternatively, the potential lack of this interaction might reflect divergent evolutionary strategies employed by these short-lived, small species with excessively long telomeres and somatic telomerase activity (Gomes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mouse telomerase RNA does not accumulate in CBs, despite the presence of a canonical CAB box in its scaRNA region.
source: In agreement with distinct telomerase trafficking regulation in human and mouse cells, mouse telomerase RNA does not accumulate in CBs, despite the presence of a canonical CAB box in its scaRNA region (Tomlinson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The HIST1H1C and hTR RNAs directly interact through the TRIAGE-P6b complementarity, resulting in an attenuation of telomere elongation by enzymatically active telomerase RNPs.
source: Collectively, our results support a model where the HIST1H1C and hTR RNAs directly interact through the TRIAGE-P6b complementarity, resulting in an attenuation of telomere elongation by enzymatically active telomerase RNPs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings and the proposed model.

claim: The findings define an entirely novel, non-coding RNA function for HIST1H1C.
source: Importantly, our findings define an entirely novel, non-coding RNA function for HIST1H1C, thus providing a glimpse into a vast space of unknown functions for coding RNAs (Tay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the findings.

claim: Telomere length is under strict negative regulatory control by various protein factors limiting telomerase action or trimming excessively long telomeres.
source: Telomere length, as a major determinant of cellular lifespan, is under strict negative regulatory control by various protein factors limiting telomerase action or trimming excessively long telomeres (Chen et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The findings identify an additional, RNA-based regulatory mechanism serving as a potential proliferative barrier to prevent unlimited cell divisions.
source: Our findings identify an additional, RNA-based regulatory mechanism serving as a potential proliferative barrier to prevent unlimited cell divisions.
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the findings.

claim: Telomerase is repressed in most human somatic cells.
source: While telomerase is repressed in most human somatic cells, its reactivation is a hallmark of malignant transformation, occurring in the majority (~80 – 90%) of cancers (Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Telomerase reactivation is a hallmark of malignant transformation, occurring in the majority (~80 – 90%) of cancers.
source: While telomerase is repressed in most human somatic cells, its reactivation is a hallmark of malignant transformation, occurring in the majority (~80 – 90%) of cancers (Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The HIST1H1C RNA-hTR interaction might constitute a tumor suppressor mechanism to curb telomere elongation even after upregulation of TERT expression.
source: By limiting the available pool of telomerase RNPs via sequestering hTR and hTR-containing complexes, the HIST1H1C RNA-hTR interaction might constitute a tumor suppressor mechanism to curb telomere elongation even after upregulation of TERT expression, and thus could contribute to the prevention of malignant transformation, for example in the adult stem cell compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the potential biological significance of the findings.

claim: The HIST1H1C RNA-hTR interaction could contribute to the prevention of malignant transformation, for example in the adult stem cell compartment.
source: By limiting the available pool of telomerase RNPs via sequestering hTR and hTR-containing complexes, the HIST1H1C RNA-hTR interaction might constitute a tumor suppressor mechanism to curb telomere elongation even after upregulation of TERT expression, and thus could contribute to the prevention of malignant transformation, for example in the adult stem cell compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the potential biological significance of the findings.

claim: Modulating telomerase activity and/or telomere elongation is an attractive and actively pursued target for cancer therapeutics.
source: Modulating telomerase activity and/or telomere elongation is an attractive and actively pursued target for cancer therapeutics (Arndt and MacKenzie, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations in genes involved in telomere maintenance result in a list of serious conditions, collectively referred to as telomeropathies.
source: On the other hand, mutations in genes involved in telomere maintenance result in a list of serious conditions, collectively referred to as telomeropathies (Holohan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Modulating the HIST1H1C-hTR RNA-RNA interaction might have significant therapeutic benefits.
source: As both aberrant telomere lengthening/maintenance and aberrant telomere shortening are of considerable clinical importance, modulating the HIST1H1C-hTR RNA-RNA interaction – either by inhibiting or mimicking/facilitating duplex formation – therefore might have significant therapeutic benefits.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The study identified ~80 RNA species interacting directly or indirectly with hTR using a targeted RNA pull-down approach.
source: Using a targeted RNA pull-down approach (Engreitz et al., 2014), we have identified ~80 RNA species interacting directly or indirectly with hTR.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: The dataset is highly enriched in mRNAs coding for proteins involved in the regulation of apoptosis.
source: In agreement with the previously published anti-apoptotic role of hTR (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014), our dataset is highly enriched in mRNAs coding for proteins involved in the regulation of apoptosis, suggesting that (some of) the extra-telomeric functions of hTR might be mediated through RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is a finding supported by the functional annotation analysis of the data.

claim: Some of the extra-telomeric functions of hTR might be mediated through RNA-RNA interactions.
source: In agreement with the previously published anti-apoptotic role of hTR (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014), our dataset is highly enriched in mRNAs coding for proteins involved in the regulation of apoptosis, suggesting that (some of) the extra-telomeric functions of hTR might be mediated through RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Only one of the mRNAs enriched upon hTR pull-down in this study (HSP90AB1) has been previously reported to interact with hTR in transcriptome-wide screens of cellular RNA-RNA interactions.
source: Interestingly, only one of the mRNAs enriched upon hTR pull-down in our study (HSP90AB1) has been previously reported to interact with hTR in transcriptome-wide screens of cellular RNA-RNA interactions (Aw et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding that compares the results with previous studies.

claim: The limited overlap with previous studies probably reflects both the insufficient saturation of transcriptome-wide methods and the biases resulting from psoralen photo-crosslinking.
source: This probably reflects both the insufficient saturation of these methods (Gong et al., 2018) and the biases resulting from psoralen photo-crosslinking (Cimino et al., 1985; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Many putative hTR-RNA duplexes do not contain uridines in a position that would conform to the substrate requirements of psoralen crosslinking.
source: Indeed, many putative hTR-RNA duplexes, including the TRIAGE-P6b interaction (Figure 3C) and the predicted scaRNA2-hTR interaction (Figure 9D), do not contain uridines in a position that would conform to the substrate requirements of psoralen crosslinking.
evidence: This is an observation based on the predicted RNA structures.

claim: Despite major technological advances in the last decade, a large fraction of the cellular RNA interactome remains unexplored.
source: As RNA molecules have an almost unlimited potential to engage in base-pairing interactions and some species accumulate only at single-digit numbers per cell, our results – in agreement with earlier targeted approaches (Engreitz et al., 2014; Kretz et al., 2013) – suggest that, despite major technological advances in the last decade, a large fraction of the cellular RNA interactome remains unexplored.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by the findings and citations to previous research.

claim: A growing number of snoRNAs and other non-coding RNAs have been shown to be further processed to various, smaller fragments and thus regulate various cellular functions in addition to their canonical roles.
source: Interestingly, in recent years, a growing number of snoRNAs and other non-coding RNAs have been shown to be further processed to various, smaller fragments and thus regulate various cellular functions in addition to their canonical roles (e.g. Falaleeva and Stamm, 2013; Kumar et al., 2016; Rogler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some of the interactions identified in the study might reflect specific functions executed by putative, hTR-derived smaller RNA species.
source: We speculate that some of the interactions identified in our study might, at least partially, reflect specific functions executed by putative, hTR-derived smaller RNA species, a possibility that remains to be addressed experimentally.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future findings.

claim: hTR selectively interacts with a small subset of scaRNAs, most prominently with scaRNA2 and scaRNA17, in both VA13-hTR and HeLa cells.
source: In addition, hTR selectively interacts with a small subset of scaRNAs – most prominently with scaRNA2 and scaRNA17 – in both VA13-hTR and HeLa cells (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the data shown in Figure 9A-C.

claim: The association with scaRNAs was significantly reduced with the m1 hTR variant that does not accumulate in CBs.
source: As expected for a specific interaction, the association with scaRNAs was significantly reduced with the m1 hTR variant (Cristofari et al., 2007; Jády et al., 2004) that does not accumulate in CBs (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the data shown in Figure 9C and consistent with previous research.

claim: scaRNA2 can potentially occupy both pseudouridylation pockets of hTR, leaving an unpaired uridine exposed (U27 and U34 for the 5' and 3' pockets, respectively).
source: By predicting base-pairing interactions between hTR and the enriched scaRNAs, we found that scaRNA2 can potentially occupy both pseudouridylation pockets of hTR, leaving an unpaired uridine exposed (U27 and U34 for the 5' and 3' pockets, respectively) (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 9D.

claim: hTR might behave as an active pseudouridylation guide RNA.
source: This suggests the exciting possibility that hTR might behave as an active pseudouridylation guide RNA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the predicted scaRNA2-hTR interaction.

claim: 35 out of 77 (45.5%) hTR-interacting mRNAs identified in VA13-hTR cells code for proteins involved in cytoskeleton organization and/or the regulation of apoptosis.
source: Strikingly, functional annotation analysis (Huang et al., 2009a; Huang et al., 2009b) showed that 35 out of 77 (45.5%) hTR-interacting mRNAs identified in VA13-hTR cells code for proteins involved in cytoskeleton organization and/or the regulation of apoptosis (Figure 8), thus providing a direct link – mediated by an intricate RNA-RNA interaction network – between hTR expression and cell survival (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the functional annotation analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The findings provide a direct link between hTR expression and cell survival mediated by an intricate RNA-RNA interaction network.
source: Strikingly, functional annotation analysis (Huang et al., 2009a; Huang et al., 2009b) showed that 35 out of 77 (45.5%) hTR-interacting mRNAs identified in VA13-hTR cells code for proteins involved in cytoskeleton organization and/or the regulation of apoptosis (Figure 8), thus providing a direct link – mediated by an intricate RNA-RNA interaction network – between hTR expression and cell survival (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional annotation analysis.

claim: Prominent hTR-associated mRNAs coding for apoptotic factors include the translationally controlled tumor protein (TCTP/TPT1) and filamin A (FLNA) RNAs.
source: Prominent hTR-associated mRNAs coding for apoptotic factors include the translationally controlled tumor protein (TCTP/TPT1) and filamin A (FLNA) RNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), ranked sixth and first in our screen, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TPT1 and FLNA proteins interact with each other and are important pleiotropic regulators of DNA repair, apoptosis, tumorigenesis, and cytoskeleton organization.
source: The two proteins interact with each other and are important pleiotropic regulators of DNA repair, apoptosis, tumorigenesis, and cytoskeleton organization (Amson et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TPT1 interacts with and regulates various apoptotic factors, including Bcl-XL and Mcl1.
source: Notably, TPT1 interacts with and regulates various apoptotic factors, including Bcl-XL (Thébault et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2005) and Mcl1 (Liu et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2002), two regulators of the Bim apoptotic pathway, which was reported to be inhibited by hTR expression (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bcl-XL and Mcl1 are two regulators of the Bim apoptotic pathway, which was reported to be inhibited by hTR expression.
source: Notably, TPT1 interacts with and regulates various apoptotic factors, including Bcl-XL (Thébault et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2005) and Mcl1 (Liu et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2002), two regulators of the Bim apoptotic pathway, which was reported to be inhibited by hTR expression (Gazzaniga and Blackburn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
